questiontext.text: What is the main difference between a constructive problem and a counting problem?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Many outputs can be valid, so the judge uses a checker. Your job is to produce any one answer that satisfies every condition.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: You must build one valid answer instead of computing a single number
Constructive problems have only one correct output

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
string s;
for (int i = 0; i < 7; i++) {
    s += 'a' + i % 3;
}
cout << s << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The remainder i % 3 repeats 0, 1, 2, so the letters cycle a, b, c, a, b, c, a. Seven letters give abcabca.

questiontext.text: Which string of length 6 over the letters a and b has no two equal neighbors?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Alternating the two letters with i % 2 always works. The others contain a pair such as aa or bb side by side.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
int n = 7;
for (int x = 2; x <= n; x += 2) cout << x << " ";
for (int x = 1; x <= n; x += 2) cout << x << " ";
cout << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The loops print the even numbers first and then the odd numbers: 2 4 6 1 3 5 7. No two neighbors differ by exactly 1, which is a classic construction.

questiontext.text: A problem asks for n distinct positive integers with sum S. What is the smallest sum that is possible?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The smallest n distinct positive integers are 1, 2, ..., n, and their sum is n × (n + 1) / 2. If S is smaller, the answer is NO.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

name.text: Q07 - Drag and drop - fill the gaps

questiontext.text:
Drag the correct value into the gap so the program prints a valid answer for n = 4 and S = 20 (the last number absorbs the rest).

main.cpp
long long n = 4, S = 20, used = 0;
for (long long i = 1; i < n; i++) {
    cout << i << " ";

}

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. The first n - 1 numbers use used = 1 + 2 + 3 = 6, so the last number is S - used = 14. The numbers 1 2 3 14 are distinct and add up to 20.

questiontext.text:
Match each term with its meaning.

Drag each description onto the item it belongs to.

Construction  →  [[1]]

Checker  →  [[2]]

Invariant  →  [[3]]

Pattern  →  [[4]]

Impossible case  →  [[5]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. A constructive solution is made of a construction and an argument (or a checker) that it works.

The correct answer:

  • Construction → A rule that builds a valid answer
  • Checker → A program that verifies a built answer
  • Invariant → A property that stays true after every step
  • Pattern → A repeating shape found in small cases
  • Impossible case → An input for which no answer exists

questiontext.text:
Sort each strategy: is it a construction tool or a verification tool?

Drag the correct label next to every item.

Periodic pattern with i % k  →  [[1]]

Checker that scans the output  →  [[2]]

Even numbers first, then odd numbers  →  [[1]]

Brute force on tiny inputs  →  [[2]]

Last element absorbs the remainder  →  [[1]]

Assert that the sum equals S  →  [[2]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. Construction tools produce the answer. Verification tools only decide whether an answer is valid. Good solvers use both.

The correct answer:

Construction tool: Periodic pattern with i % k, Even numbers first, then odd numbers, Last element absorbs the remainder
Verification tool: Checker that scans the output, Brute force on tiny inputs, Assert that the sum equals S

questiontext.text: Why can a sum parity argument prove that some inputs have no answer?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. If every piece changes the total by an even amount, an odd target can never be reached. Such an argument proves impossibility without trying anything.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: An odd or even total may be impossible to reach with the allowed pieces, however you arrange them
Because even numbers are always larger
Because the judge rejects odd numbers
Because parity only matters for strings

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
int n = 5;
vector<int> p(n);
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    p[i] = (i + 2) % n + 1;
}
for (int v : p) cout << v << " ";
cout << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. A cyclic shift of 1..5 by 2 positions gives 3 4 5 1 2. Every number appears exactly once, so it is a permutation.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text: You need a permutation of 1..n in which no element stays in its original position (a derangement). Which construction works for n ≥ 2?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. A cyclic shift by one moves every element to a new position, and it contains each number once. The identity keeps every element fixed.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: Shift every element one place cyclically

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
vector<int> a = {3, 1, 2};
bool ok = true;
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    if (a[i] == i + 1) ok = false;
}
cout << (ok ? "valid" : "invalid") << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. This checker looks for a fixed point. The values 3, 1, 2 differ from the positions 1, 2, 3 everywhere, so the permutation is valid.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text: Why is a checker useful even after you have proved your construction?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. A proof shows that the idea is correct, but a bug can still break the code. Running the checker on many small inputs catches those bugs.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: It catches coding mistakes that the proof does not show
It makes the program run faster
It replaces the need for reading the problem

questiontext.text:
Arrange the steps of the "last element absorbs the rest" construction.

Drag the steps into the correct order.

1. [[1]]

2. [[2]]

3. [[3]]

4. [[4]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. The impossible case is rejected first. The last number is larger than n - 1, so it is automatically different from the others.

The correct answer:

  1. Check that S is at least the minimum possible sum
  2. Print the first n - 1 numbers 1, 2, ..., n - 1
  3. Compute the sum of the printed numbers
  4. Print S minus that sum as the last number

questiontext.text:
Match each construction with the property it guarantees.

Drag each description onto the item it belongs to.

i % 2 alternation  →  [[1]]

Cyclic shift of 1..n  →  [[2]]

Evens first, then odds  →  [[3]]

1, 2, ..., n-1 and a big last number  →  [[4]]

Repeat the pattern abc  →  [[5]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. Each tool is simple, but it guarantees exactly one useful property.

The correct answer:

  • i % 2 alternation → No two neighbors are equal
  • Cyclic shift of 1..n → A permutation with no fixed point
  • Evens first, then odds → A simple split by parity
  • 1, 2, ..., n-1 and a big last number → Distinct values with an exact sum
  • Repeat the pattern abc → A string with period 3

questiontext.text:
Sort each statement: is it a good habit when solving constructive problems?

Drag the correct label next to every item.

Solve n = 1, 2, 3 by hand first  →  [[1]]

Submit the first idea without testing  →  [[2]]

Write a checker for the conditions  →  [[1]]

Assume the pattern from one example  →  [[2]]

Prove why impossible inputs are impossible  →  [[1]]

Ignore the smallest inputs  →  [[2]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. Small cases and checkers expose wrong ideas early. A pattern seen in one example may be a coincidence.

The correct answer:

Good habit: Solve n = 1, 2, 3 by hand first, Write a checker for the conditions, Prove why impossible inputs are impossible
Bad habit: Submit the first idea without testing, Assume the pattern from one example, Ignore the smallest inputs
